title: YuanChen(Cary) Ling
text: Hi! My name is YuanChen (Cary) Ling, and I am originally from China. Before joining the MDS program, I completed my undergraduate degree at the University of Toronto, where I majored in Mathematics and Statistics. My career goal is to become a professional data analyst, and I hope to pursue this path after graduating from the MDS program. Outside of data science, I am also passionate about DJing and breaking—maybe they could even become part-time careers someday, who knows?

title: R and Python Together
text:
This post demonstrates how R and Python can work together in the same Quarto document. First, I create an object in R and then use that object in Python.

library(reticulate)

life_expectancy <- c(68.8, 73.4, 75.2, 70.1, 77.5)

life_expectancy

[1] 68.8 73.4 75.2 70.1 77.5

title: R and Python Together
section: Passing Data from R to Python
text:
Passing Data from R to Python
The R object life_expectancy is passed to Python using r.life_expectancy.

import numpy as np

life_exp_python = np.array(r.life_expectancy)

mean_life_expectancy = life_exp_python.mean()

mean_life_expectancy

np.float64(73.0)

title: R and Python Together
section: Passing the Result Back to R
text:
Passing the Result Back to R
The mean calculated in Python can be accessed from R using py$mean_life_expectancy.

mean_from_python <- py$mean_life_expectancy

mean_from_python

[1] 73

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
My first few weeks in MDS have been exciting but also stressful. There are many lectures, labs, worksheets, and assignments, and each course covers a lot of material in a short time. I am still getting used to the fast pace and learning how to manage my time better.
So far, I have learned many new topics and tools. In Python and R, I have worked with programming, data manipulation, and data cleaning. I have also studied probability and statistics while learning tools such as Git, GitHub, the command line, and Quarto.
One of my biggest concerns is finding a job after graduation. Since MDS is a short and intensive program, I feel that I need to prepare for the job market while keeping up with my courses. My goal is to become a data analyst, and I hope the skills I learn in MDS will help me achieve that goal.



A moment from UBC

title: Analysis of Penguins
text:
Average Body Mass by Species
Next, I compare the average body mass of the three penguin species.

body_mass_by_species = (
    penguins.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"]
    .mean()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
)

title: Analysis of Penguins
text:
Summary of Penguin Measurements
Finally, I summarize the body mass and flipper length for each penguin species.

penguin_summary = (
    penguins.groupby("species")
    .agg(
        mean_body_mass=("body_mass_g", "mean"),
        mean_flipper_length=("flipper_length_mm", "mean"),
        number_of_penguins=("species", "count")
    )
    .round(2)
)

title: Analysis of Gapminder
text:
Average Life Expectancy by Continent
To compare life expectancy across continents, I calculate the mean life expectancy for each continent.

life_exp_by_continent <- gapminder |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(
    mean_life_exp = mean(lifeExp)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_life_exp))

life_exp_by_continent

title: Analysis of Gapminder
section: GDP per Capita and Life Expectancy
text:
GDP per Capita and Life Expectancy
Next, I visualize the relationship between GDP per capita and life expectancy. Each point represents a country in a particular year, and colors distinguish continents.

ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "GDP per Capita",
    y = "Life Expectancy",
    color = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Relationship between GDP per capita and life expectancy across continents.






Data Source
The data used in this analysis come from the gapminder R package. The dataset contains country-level information on life expectancy, population, and GDP per capita across multiple years.
